title: Section check: Who builds AI, and at what cost
intro: 8 questions about Lessons 5–8. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: Like clothes, an AI tool has a supply chain. What is a supply chain?

options.text: The people who help make it, step by step
options.feedback: Yes. A supply chain is all the people and places that help to make a product. Some of them stay hidden.

options.text: A list of rules that say how the tool must work
options.feedback: Not quite. Rules are not a supply chain. A supply chain is the people who help make a product. Look back at Lesson 5.

options.text: A shop where people can buy the tool
options.feedback: Not quite. A shop sells a product. A supply chain is all the people who help to make it. Look back at Lesson 5.

questions.question: In 2023, Oxford researchers checked 15 online work platforms. What did they find?

options.text: Every platform paid all workers fairly
options.feedback: Not quite. The researchers found low pay and a lot of unpaid time. Look back at Lesson 5.

options.text: Workers were paid for every hour they spent
options.feedback: Not quite. More than a quarter of the workers' time was unpaid, such as time looking for tasks. Look back at Lesson 5.

options.text: None met all of their basic standards
options.feedback: Yes. The best platform scored only 5 out of 10. Some platforms changed their rules after the study.

questions.question: Why do many data centres use water?

options.text: To make the power that the chips use
options.feedback: Not quite. Data centres use a lot of electricity, but the water does not make it. Look back at Lesson 6.

options.text: To cool chips that get very hot
options.feedback: Yes. The chips use a lot of electricity and get very hot. Water helps to cool them.

options.text: To wash the dust off the computers
options.feedback: Not quite. The water is not for cleaning. It helps with the heat. Look back at Lesson 6.

stimulus.title: A made-up data centre plan
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. A company plans a data centre in the made-up town of Westvale. It says about 800 people will help to build it over two years. About 40 people will work there after it opens.

questions.question: A man in the town says, “This will give 800 people work for years.” What is wrong with this?

options.text: The building work lasts only two years
options.feedback: Yes. Building work ends when the building is finished. After that, there are only about 40 jobs.

options.text: Data centres need nobody to build them
options.feedback: Not quite. The company says about 800 people will help to build it. Look back at Lesson 6.

options.text: All 800 people will work inside it later
options.feedback: Not quite. Only about 40 people will work there after it opens. Look back at Lesson 6.

questions.question: In Harbourside, few people publish books in Language C. What does “publish” mean?

options.text: To speak a language at home
options.feedback: Not quite. People speak Language C a lot. To publish means to put out writing. Look back at Lesson 7.

options.text: To change words into another language
options.feedback: Not quite. That is to translate. To publish is to put out writing for many people. Look back at Lesson 7.

options.text: To put out writing for many to read
options.feedback: Yes. To publish is to print or put out writing. Little is published in Language C, so AI has little to learn from.

questions.question: Why do some languages have much more writing than others?

options.text: Some languages are much harder to write
options.feedback: Not quite. It is not about how hard a language is. It depends on how a language has been used. Look back at Lesson 7.

options.text: History, such as which ones schools use
options.feedback: Yes. It depends on history: which languages schools, books, news and governments use, and what people type online.

options.text: The more speakers, the more writing
options.feedback: Not quite. In Harbourside, Language C has the most speakers but very little writing. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.question: About 45% of a famous photo collection came from the United States, and about 2% from India. What does this help to explain?

options.text: Why a tool did worse with photos from India
options.feedback: Yes. Few photos came from India, so the data did not represent it well. A tool trained on it did worse there.

options.text: Why the tool did better with photos from India
options.feedback: Not quite. With so few photos from India, the tool did worse there, not better. Look back at Lesson 8.

options.text: Why people in India took fewer photos
options.feedback: Not quite. The numbers show what is in the collection. They do not show how many photos people took. Look back at Lesson 8.

stimulus.title: A made-up fish tool
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. At the made-up Stonebay market, a tool names fish from photos. It names river fish well, but it often gets sea fish wrong. Almost all of its training photos show river fish.

questions.question: What would most likely help the tool?

options.text: Add more photos of river fish
options.feedback: Not quite. It already knows river fish well. More of the same kind will not fill the gap. Look back at Lesson 8.

options.text: Add labelled photos of sea fish
options.feedback: Yes. Its training data does not represent sea fish. Labelled photos of sea fish can fill that gap.

options.text: Use the tool only when it is sunny
options.feedback: Not quite. The light is not the problem. The problem is what its training photos show. Look back at Lesson 8.

results.high: Well done. You can see the people, the planet and the languages behind AI tools.
results.middle: Good work. You got many questions right. Look back at the lessons for the ones you missed, and try again if you like.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 5–8, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
